title: Ezra 9:5–15
context: At the evening offering Ezra kneels with hands spread out to the LORD and prays. He confesses that the community’s guilt has risen to the heavens, recalls the exile as the result of the people’s sins, and acknowledges that God has shown a brief moment of grace by leaving a remnant, giving them a secure hold in his holy place and reviving them under the kings of Persia. He then confesses that they have broken the commands given through the prophets not to intermarry with the peoples of the land, asks whether they will again provoke God until no remnant is left, and ends by declaring God righteous and the people guilty before him. The prayer is kept intact as one unit.

verses.text: At the evening offering I rose up from my humiliation, even with my garment and my robe torn; and I fell on my knees, and spread out my hands to the LORD my God;
verses.arminianNotes: At the evening offering Ezra rises, kneels, and spreads his hands to the LORD. Arminian readers note that he times his prayer with the regular worship of the temple, joining personal grief to the community’s sacrifice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the posture of kneeling with hands spread as humble dependence on God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the beginning of a prayer of confession, offered publicly before God’s house.

verses.text: and I said, “My God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have increased over our head, and our guiltiness has grown up to the heavens.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra says he is ashamed to lift his face, for iniquities have risen over their heads and guilt to the heavens. Arminian readers see sincere confession that speaks in the first person plural, including himself with the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the confession a recognition of the depth of sin before a holy God. Both traditions read the opening as a model of corporate confession, in which a leader owns the sin of the community as his own.

verses.text: Since the days of our fathers we have been exceedingly guilty to this day; and for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plunder, and to confusion of face, as it is this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra confesses that since their fathers’ days they have been guilty, and that kings and priests were given into the hands of foreign kings. Arminian readers note that he reads the exile as the consequence of persistent unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exile as God’s just judgment, as the prophets had warned. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing the present crisis within the long history of Israel’s sin and God’s discipline.

verses.text: Now for a little moment grace has been shown from the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant to escape, and to give us a stake in his holy place, that our God may lighten our eyes, and revive us a little in our bondage.
verses.arminianNotes: For a little moment grace has been shown, leaving a remnant and giving a secure hold in God’s holy place. Arminian readers see the remnant as a gracious gift; on wider questions of remnant and election, see the existing boxes at Romans 11:5 and Isaiah 1:9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s undeserved favor in preserving a remnant and reviving his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for grace, and neither adds a new contrast here; the existing boxes already set out their differences.

verses.text: For we are bondservants; yet our God has not forsaken us in our bondage, but has extended loving kindness to us in the sight of the kings of Persia, to revive us, to set up the house of our God, and to repair its ruins, and to give us a wall in Judah and in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Though they are bondservants, God has not forsaken them, but has shown loving kindness before the kings of Persia. Arminian readers note that God’s faithfulness is seen through the favor of foreign rulers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence moving Persian kings to allow the temple’s rebuilding and a wall in Judah. Both traditions read the verse as gratitude for God’s steadfast love, with the wall often taken as a picture of protection rather than a literal structure.

verses.text: “Now, our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra asks what they can say after this, for they have forsaken God’s commandments. Arminian readers note the turn from grace received to sin committed, which makes the people’s failure more grievous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as acknowledging that no excuse is possible before God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the hinge of the prayer, moving from God’s kindness to the people’s confession of guilt.

verses.text: which you have commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, ‘The land to which you go to possess is an unclean land through the uncleanness of the peoples of the lands, through their abominations, which have filled it from one end to another with their filthiness.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra recalls commands given through the prophets that the land was unclean through the abominations of its peoples. Arminian readers note that the wording draws together themes from passages such as Leviticus 18:24–28 rather than quoting a single text.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the concern as moral and religious defilement through false worship. Both traditions read the verse as grounding the issue in covenant holiness, and they avoid applying it to peoples or ethnic groups today.

verses.text: Now therefore don’t give your daughters to their sons. Don’t take their daughters to your sons, nor seek their peace or their prosperity forever, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land, and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.’
verses.arminianNotes: The commands forbid giving daughters to their sons or taking their daughters, and seeking their peace and prosperity. Arminian readers note the link to Deuteronomy 7:3 and 23:6, where the concern is that Israel would be turned from the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the commands as protecting Israel’s covenant identity and inheritance in the land. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse within Israel’s historical covenant setting, not as a general rule about marriage across peoples.

verses.text: “After all that has come on us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, since you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and have given us such a remnant,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra says God has punished them less than their iniquities deserve and has given them a remnant. Arminian readers see God’s mercy as tempering his justice, giving the people room to repent and return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lighter punishment as sheer grace, not owed to the people in any way. Both traditions read the verse as confessing that the present remnant exists because of God’s mercy, a point they fully share.

verses.text: shall we again break your commandments, and join ourselves with the peoples that do these abominations? Wouldn’t you be angry with us until you had consumed us, so that there would be no remnant, nor any to escape?
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra asks whether they will again break God’s commands and join with peoples who do these abominations, risking complete destruction. Arminian readers see a real danger that continued unfaithfulness could bring final judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as a solemn warning that drives the people to repentance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as expressing fear of God’s anger, and see the warning as meant to move the community to faithfulness.

verses.text: LORD, the God of Israel, you are righteous; for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guiltiness; for no one can stand before you because of this.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra declares that the LORD is righteous and that the people stand guilty before him, for no one can stand because of this. Arminian readers see honest confession that offers no excuse and casts the people on God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the acknowledgment of God’s righteousness and human guilt as the right posture before a holy God. Both traditions read the prayer’s ending as leaving the outcome with God, without a request for anything but his mercy.
